packages/reactive-audio/src/timing.ts.content:
`BigInt(Math.round(latencyMs * 1e6))` throws a `RangeError` when `latencyMs` is non-finite (`NaN`/`Infinity`), and the result of the subtraction is never guarded. Two failure modes here:
1. A bad `LatencyMeasurement` (e.g., deserialized qualification record, or `detectedAtMs - emittedAtMs` that somehow becomes non-finite) stored via `record()` will make `align()`/`alignFeature()` throw at runtime instead of failing safe.
2. When the offset exceeds `captureTimeNs` (capture near stream start, or an over-measured offset) `showTimeNs` underflows to a negative `bigint`, which the correlation (T-LIVE-07) and adaptive clock (DS-23) consumers may treat as an invalid timestamp.
Validate the input and clamp/handle the result.

`record()` stores any `LatencyMeasurement` without validating `latencyMs` or `confidence`. A negative/non-finite `latencyMs` violates the `alignedShowTimeNs` contract ("subtracted, never added") — a negative value shifts show time forward and can crash `align()` via `BigInt`; a `confidence` outside [0, 1] silently propagates incorrect calibration quality downstream. Validate before accepting.

When `detectedAtMs < emittedAtMs` the difference is silently clamped to 0 with no signal to the caller, so an inverted emission/detection ordering or a clock-domain skew is presented as a valid zero-latency measurement. `confidence` is then computed against the clamped 0 (denominator `Math.max(1, 0)`), over-reporting calibration quality for a physically impossible result. Consider surfacing the inversion (e.g., return a sentinel or throw) rather than masking it.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/link.test.ts.content: The publish-wait loop recurses via `setImmediate` with no iteration cap or deadline. If `publish()` never produces a `setTempo` frame (e.g. the socket is closed, the write is dropped, or a future gating flag suppresses publishing), `published.promise` never settles and the whole suite hangs instead of failing with a clear message. Bound the loop with a deadline/attempt count and throw on timeout. Returning the matched line (see next comment) also lets the assertion validate the payload.

The only check is that the received text contains the substring `setTempo`; the actual value (126) is never asserted. A publish path that writes a wrong or malformed tempo (e.g. `setTempo: 0`, `NaN`, or a string) would still pass. Parse the frame and assert the full payload.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/link.test.ts.content: The transport is only stopped inside the `try` block; the `finally` closes only the fake server. If any assertion before `transport.stop()` throws, the client socket stays open and leaks into later tests. Worse, `stopFakeSidecar` calls `server.close()`, whose callback only fires once all existing connections have ended, so with the transport socket still open the `finally` itself can hang. Move `transport.stop()` into the `finally` (guarding against a double-stop) so teardown always runs.

packages/serato/src/emulator.ts.content: `close()` can hang forever: it attaches a `'close'` listener and then calls `socket.end()`. If the socket has already been destroyed/closed (e.g. a connection error before or after `connect()` resolved, or the peer closed first), the `'close'` event has already been emitted and will never fire again, so `await promise` never settles and the test process hangs. Guard against the already-closed state (or race with a timeout).

`this.socket?.write(...)` silently no-ops when `socket` is null (never connected, or already nulled by `close()`). A script can therefore "play" successfully while emitting zero frames, and tests can pass without ever exercising the protocol. Consider throwing when there is no live socket so the failure is surfaced instead of hidden.

packages/serato/src/emulator.ts.content: The `'error'` handler only rejects the `connect()` promise. Once the promise has settled, calling `reject` is a no-op, so all later socket errors (during handshake/playback) are swallowed with no cleanup and no propagation. Pending `awaiters` are left to time out after 4s instead of failing fast, and the caller never learns the connection broke. Store the error / reject pending waiters (see also `awaitPredicate`/`close`).

`setTimeout` here is never cleared, and waiters are only removed on match or timeout. A successful match leaves the timer alive (keeping the event loop busy for up to 4s), and on socket close/error the pending promise is neither resolved nor rejected, so callers see a generic 4s 'no ... from server' timeout instead of the real disconnect cause. Capture the timer handle and clear it on settle, and add a way to fail/reject outstanding waiters when the socket errors or closes. Also consider hoisting the hardcoded 4000 ms into a named constant.

The handshake couples success to the server sending `/Register/Status/Video/Mixer/Crossfader` and to that frame being the *last* one of the subscription burst. If the server subscribes to a different topic set, or emits the crossfader topic earlier/mid-burst, the topic list read back after this await is incomplete and the caller instead gets a generic 4s timeout rather than a clear protocol-mismatch error. Also, `register` is redundant: the first `/Register/Status/` address returned by `awaitMessagePrefix` is already contained in the filtered `receivedMessages` list, so `[...new Set([register, ...])]` would be identical without it.

Extract a small helper (e.g. `filepathMessage(deckId, filePath)`) to remove the duplication and the unsafe cast.

packages/storage/src/logging.ts.content: The spread order `...this.sessionFields(), ...extra` lets caller-supplied `extra` override the logger's own core fields (`timestamp`, `monoMs`, `module`, `severity`, `message`). Since `extra` is typed `Partial<LogFields>`, a caller (or forwarded worker payload) can silently replace these, producing records that no longer reflect this logger or the spec-130 schema. Build core fields last, or strip reserved keys from `extra` before spreading.

`state.suppressed` is incremented but never read anywhere, and `onSuppressed` is always invoked with the constant `1`. Consumers cannot distinguish a burst of N suppressed lines from N separate single suppressions, and any intent to report an accumulated count per window is never realized (the field is effectively dead). Also, the accumulated count is never flushed when the key changes or the window rolls over. Either surface `state.suppressed` (and reset it) when reporting, or drop the unused field.

The dedup key is only `${severity}:${message}`, ignoring contextual fields (`session`, `deck`, `track`, `fixture`, `event`). Two genuinely distinct events that share severity+message (e.g. the same error text for different decks/tracks) are treated as repeats and silently dropped within the window, causing real data loss. Include the contextual identifiers in the key (or require callers to make messages unique).

`timestamp` is derived from `monoMs` via `new Date(monoMs)`. The field name (and injectable `now`) implies a monotonic clock; if a caller injects `performance.now()` or another monotonic source, `monoMs` is not wall-clock epoch ms, so `timestamp` becomes a wrong (1970-based) time while still passing validation. Additionally, if `now()` returns an out-of-range value, `toISOString()` throws `RangeError`. Capture wall-clock time for `timestamp` independently (or document/enforce that `now` must be `Date.now`).

Required fields are validated individually above and then re-checked by this loop, so a single missing field yields two problems (e.g. `timestamp: missing or not an ISO date` plus `timestamp: missing`). This pollutes diagnostics and makes problem counts misleading. The core-field presence checks are redundant with the individual checks — drop this loop (or drop the presence clause from the individual checks).

This only checks for the *presence* of `rawProtocol`; it never validates its type. In diagnostic mode a `rawProtocol` of any type (number, object, etc.) passes validation, contradicting the `LogFields.rawProtocol?: string` contract and potentially breaking downstream consumers that assume a string. Validate the type when the key is present.

packages/storage/src/perf.test.ts.content: The deliberately injected stall is a single-tick event, so its pass/fail is evaluated with `statistic: "p99"`. Whether the stall lands in p99 depends on how many catch-up ticks the drift-corrected loop emits above the threshold after the busy-wait (here it just barely does, ~5 samples of ~201 exceed 15 ms, needing at least 3). A slightly different sample count or scheduler behaviour pushes the outlier outside p99, the measurement passes, and `failedMeasurements(...)` no longer equals `["showHost.tickJitterWith20msStall"]`. Use `statistic: "max"` (as the `jitter?.max` assertion already relies on) or make the stall span enough ticks to deterministically enter p99.

This assertion requires the injected stall to be the only failing measurement, but the non-stall measurements use host-dependent wall-clock timings. On a loaded host render/IPC/DJ can exceed even the relaxed 3x thresholds (the file's own comment notes a dev host measuring ~6.7 ms against a 3x10 ms-ish budget), so `failedMeasurements` may contain extra names and the test fails spuriously; conversely a genuine regression on a fast host can slip under the slack. The assertion is therefore both flaky and weak as a regression gate — consider asserting that the stall entry is among the failures (or pin deterministic/mocked timing) rather than exact equality.
